title: Red Meat and Colorectal Cancer: A Quantitative Update on the State of the Epidemiologic Science
authors: Alexander DD, Weed DL, Miller PE, Mohamed MA
journal: Journal of the American College of Nutrition
population: 27 independent prospective cohort studies published to 2013
funder: This manuscript was partially funded by Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA). MLA did not contribute to the writing, analysis, or interpretation of study findings.
authorConflicts: Authors affiliated with EpidStat Institute, DLW Consulting Services and Doctors Without Borders; no conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
result: High against low red meat intake, 27 cohorts: summary relative risk 1.11 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.19), heterogeneity P = 0.014, I2 33.6%. Associations attenuated in models of fresh red meat separated from processed meat, in better adjusted models, in women and outside the United States. Categories of median intake above 100 g/day (6 studies): 1.20 (1.11 to 1.29); categories up to 100 g/day 1.00 to 1.03, not significant; each 70 g increment (13 studies) 1.05 (0.97 to 1.13). The authors conclude that red meat intake does not appear to be an independent predictor of colorectal cancer risk.
